Commander night at Alex's house on Moraga Way in Orinda, Friday 28 August. Three-player pod: me, Alex, Stuart. Game three of four on the night.

Good hand, dense interaction, and I countered at the right moments — the deck did the thing it is built to do and still lost.

The archetype's own problem showed up plainly: making everyone draw also hands everyone answers to my counters. I am symmetrically fuelling the table's ability to fight me.

I lost the game losing Heliod, in a stack war. I countered a spell, Alex countered my counter; I cast Swords to Plowshares, Alex redirected it onto Heliod. Engine offline from there. Psychosis Crawler was on the battlefield with the pieces to grow it and I never got there.

The read is that the deck has TOO MANY AXES and not enough of any one of them. There are sharp concepts in here and I still believe in the shell, but it is spread thin.

WHAT IT NEEDS IS PROTECTION. Losing the commander takes the whole engine down and there is currently no answer to a counter war plus redirected removal. That is the rebuild direction: protection first, before adding any more axes.

Commander night at Oliver's, Tuesday 8 September, four-player: Sean, Oliver
(Cranko), Alex (fight deck), Ryan (Scorpion King). Second game I played that
night.

Kept about three lands, Smothering Tithe, a creature and Long-Term Plans. Got
the Tithe down early alongside Kami of the Crescent Moon and was netting about
three treasure a cycle.

THE OPTICS. Tithe made me the target immediately and I had no creatures out.
The lesson is to have a shell or blockers around Tithe, or defer deploying it
until I do.

THE SEQUENCING ERRORS, and there were three:

1. Supreme Verdict after Heliod was already out. I killed my own commander.
   Wipe first, then resolve Heliod.

2. I sat on Long-Term Plans. I should have tutored Approach of the Second Sun
   to third-from-top immediately. I was overthinking the mana cost — with the
   treasure and the discount it is two or three, not seven. I waited, got
   desperate, and the window closed.

3. I played the channel-tutor spirit as a blocker instead of using it to tutor.
   I got caught between "I am getting beaten up" and "I need to assemble my win
   condition", and I took the short-term survival play.

There is no pressure to rush the commander out in this build and I keep acting
as though there is.

Oliver assembled his one-card Cranko line while the table beat on me. Loss.
One- and two-card combo lines take the piloting element out of it, which is not
my style — though the pod is competitive and that is the room I am in.

DECK READ: I like the Approach build-around and the "live long enough" plan,
and I want to play Heliod more. Research: more ways to convert opponents' card
draw into value. The hand-size punisher axis needed too many pieces and only
ever pinged.

CROSS-GAME: momentum, tempo and table optics are the recurring gap, and it is
me rather than the decks. I avoid Heliod partly because blue-white control feels
intimidating and partly out of table-match consideration.

Pilot's Log — Nov 3, 2026, Oliver's 5-Player Pod

Session summary
Record 1–1. Heliod won game 1 on Approach of the Second Sun; Sharknado lost game 2 to Ryan's T'Vol going infinite around turn 8–9. First five-player pod in a while, and the table stepped up to bracket 4.

Table, game 1: Sean, Heliod (WIN). Oliver, Veto — lifegain / drain. Ryan, Abigail (high bracket 3). Alex, Blue-black deck. Tom, Not recalled.

Heliod closed without Heliod. The commander was removed early and the Approach line won on tutors + Dig Through Time alone. The piloting gap was giving up on the commander line too soon, not the deck.

Game 1 — Heliod (WIN, Approach of the Second Sun)
Won by casting Approach twice, under a clock, after Heliod was removed and the commander line abandoned.
How it went
• Early game was the deck's best case: Rhystic Study plus a no-maximum-hand-size effect put 25–30 cards in hand. Ryan said he didn't mind the draw because Sean "gets lost in the sauce" with that many cards.
• Ryan cast an Armageddon effect. Sean held a counterspell and countered it to keep his lands. Ryan answered by removing Heliod before any protection was equipped.
• With the commander gone, Sean committed fully to Approach: spent all mana on tutors, cast Dig Through Time off delve for two mana (six cards in graveyard), took Approach, and cast it with the remaining mana plus a one-mana white discount from an artifact.
• Table is explosive at bracket 4; the pilot read it as a clock and raced. The race paid off.
Decision points
Counter the Armageddon — Kept lands; drew removal onto Heliod — Possible misstep. Smothering Tithe was in hand — letting Armageddon resolve and casting Tithe while the table rebuilt would have left Sean alone with mana.
Abandon the Heliod line after removal — Never recast Heliod (2 tax) — Gave up too soon. Hand was full of flash-speed and generic-discount cards built around the transformed Heliod; none were cast.
Go all-in on Approach — Won — Stands by it. The clock was real and the line closed.
Notes for the workbench
• Both alternative lines (Tithe after Armageddon; recast Heliod and play the discount hand) were available and unused. The deck gave the pilot three ways to win; he saw one.
• Protection on Heliod still has to land before the table is provoked. A counterspell on a table-favourite card is a provocation.

Heliod — pilot's manual notes
• Add a decision rule for the Armageddon spot: with Tithe in hand, letting a mass land-destruction spell resolve can be the stronger line.
• Add a rule against abandoning the commander line after one removal. Recasting at 2 tax with a discount-and-flash hand is usually still the best play, even while assembling Approach.
• Protection must be on Heliod before the pilot counters a table-favourite spell.
No list changes yet.
